en: East Line Convenience had been gone for years.
A Vietnamese restaurant occupied the site now.
But the clerk who worked there in 1998 still lived in Rivermere.
His name was Samir Patel. Sixty-one. Owner of a small grocery in the south end. Nora found him behind the counter opening a case of bottled water.
"Haven't heard that name in a long time."
"You told police you saw her around seven on the night of the fire."
Samir thought for a long moment.
"I remember a woman coming in for coffee."
"Knew her face. She came over from Halden sometimes."
"Took her money. Talked about weather. That kind of knowing."
Nora showed him Lena's employee photograph.
"Are you one hundred percent certain that's the woman who came in that night?"
"You're asking for one hundred percent after twenty-eight years?"
"Police showed me a picture. Asked if that was the woman. I said she looked like her."
"She wore a knit cap. It was cold."
"You reporters always think people leave dying declarations when they buy coffee."
She was almost at the door when Samir called after her.
"I remember she had a blue bag."
"She almost spilled coffee on it when she set the cup down. She seemed nervous."
That evening, Nora found his original statement at Martin's house.
There was no mention of a blue document case.
Subject carried dark folder or purse, uncertain.
Nora took a photograph from her bag.
It had been taken in the summer of 1997. Mara stood beside a lake, slim, long black hair loose over her shoulders.
"She and Lena look alike?" Nora asked.
"Through a convenience-store window. In a knit cap. Wearing the same coat-"
Nora placed Lena's employee photograph beside Mara's.
They did not look like sisters.
Lena had a rounder face. Mara's chin was sharper. But they were nearly the same height, both had dark hair, and there were only three years between them.
If a witness recognized a coat, a silhouette, and a half-remembered face-
Nora said, "I'm thinking the woman who walked into East Line at 19:06 may never have been Lena."
"Then who was at the fax machine at 19:18?"
Nora looked at the three notes on the wall.
Martin crossed the room and removed the notes.
"Because we don't know it was one woman."
For the first time, they no longer sat on a single line.
zh: East Line便利店已经不存在了。
原址现在是一家越南餐厅。
但1998年的店员还在里弗米尔。
他的名字叫Samir Patel，六十一岁，在南区经营一家小型杂货店。诺拉找到他时，他正站在收银台后拆一箱瓶装水。
“这个名字我很多年没听过了。”
“你当年告诉警方，火灾那天晚上七点左右见过她。”
诺拉拿出Lena当年的员工照片。
“你百分之百确定那晚进来的是她？”
“二十八年前的事，你让我说百分之百？”
“警察拿照片来。他们问是不是这个女人。我说，看起来是。”
“你们记者总觉得人二十八年前买咖啡时会留下遗言。”
“我记得她那天手里拿着一个蓝色袋子。”
“因为她把咖啡放柜台上时差点弄湿它。她很紧张。”
诺拉当天晚上在Martin家找到了原始证词。
只有一句：Subject carried dark folder or purse, uncertain。
“不确定是文件夹还是手袋。”Martin说。
诺拉从包里拿出一张照片。
Mara站在湖边，黑色长发，身形纤细。
“如果隔着便利店玻璃，戴帽子，穿同一件外套——”
她把Lena员工照和Mara照片并排放在桌上。
Lena脸更圆，Mara下巴更尖。但身高接近，都是黑发，年龄只差三岁。如果一个证人只认识制服、背影和一个模糊的脸——
“我在想，十九点零六分出现在便利店的人，也许从来就不是Lena。”
诺拉看向墙上三张便签。
Martin走过去，把三张便签取下来。
“因为我们还不知道是不是一个人。”
他说着，把三张便签隔开。
第一次，不再把它们排在同一条线上。
